_about: The one source for which snakes SnakeList calls venomous. tools/venom_status.py writes it into the app's cards (data-venomous and the red Venomous tag); everything else - the app's filters, tags, quick look, quiz and map, the species pages' key facts and tags, the genus, family, country and region pages - reads the cards. Elapidae, Viperidae and Atractaspididae were already venomous in the cards. Harm to people (Venomous vs Mildly venomous) is the app's #harm-data: a venomous snake that is not on it is shown as Mildly venomous. Rear-fanged (opisthoglyphous) snakes listed here produce venom from a Duvernoy's (oral) gland and deliver it through enlarged, often grooved, teeth at the back of the upper jaw; most are harmless to people.

_sources.weinstein2011: Weinstein, S.A., Warrell, D.A., White, J. & Keyler, D.E. (2011) 'Venomous' Bites from 'Non-Venomous' Snakes: A Critical Analysis of Risk and Management of 'Colubrid' Snake Bites. Elsevier.
_sources.rdb: The Reptile Database (reptile-database.reptarium.cz), genus and species accounts
_sources.wp: Wikipedia genus and species articles (each cited on the species pages that use them)
_sources.mackessy2002: Mackessy, S.P. (2002) Biochemistry and pharmacology of colubrid snake venoms. Journal of Toxicology: Toxin Reviews 21: 43-83.

Homalopsidae.why: Indo-Australian mud and water snakes: the whole family is rear-fanged and venomous (mildly, to people)

Psammophiidae.why: Sand snakes, skaapstekers and relatives: the whole family is rear-fanged and venomous

Ahaetulla.why: Asian vine snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Dryophiops.why: Whip snakes related to Ahaetulla: rear-fanged

Telescopus.why: Cat snakes (tiger snakes of Africa): rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Oxybelis.why: American vine snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Tantilla.why: Centipede and black-headed snakes: small grooved rear fangs and a mild venom used on centipedes

Macroprotodon.why: False smooth snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Hypsiglena.why: Night snakes: mild venom from enlarged rear teeth

Imantodes.why: Blunt-headed tree snakes: rear-fanged, very mild venom

Oxyrhopus.why: False coral and flame snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Xenodon.why: Toad-eating false vipers: enlarged rear fangs, mild envenoming recorded

Helicops.why: Keelback water snakes of South America: rear-fanged, envenoming recorded

Thamnodynastes.why: Neotropical swamp snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Coniophanes.why: Black-striped snakes: rear-fanged, mild envenoming recorded

Phalotris.why: Reticulated collared snakes: rear-fanged, envenoming recorded

Leioheterodon.why: Malagasy hognose snakes: rear-fanged, mild envenoming recorded

Langaha.why: Malagasy leaf-nosed snakes: rear-fanged, mildly venomous

Ithycyphus.why: Malagasy tree snakes: rear-fanged, envenoming recorded

Amplorhinus.why: Many-spotted reed snake: rear-fanged, mild envenoming recorded

reviewed_not_changed.Heterodon: Hognose snakes have enlarged rear teeth and a Duvernoy's secretion, but SnakeList's sourced account calls the Eastern Hognose non-venomous; left as non-venomous until an expert source is added to its account
reviewed_not_changed.Thamnophis: Garter snakes: an oral secretion that is mildly toxic to prey; standard field guides call them non-venomous. Left as non-venomous
reviewed_not_changed.Erythrolamprus: Some species have enlarged rear teeth and a few envenomings are reported, but not for the genus as a whole. Left as non-venomous
reviewed_not_changed.Apostolepis: Rear-fanged burrowers with little bite information. Left as non-venomous pending a source
reviewed_not_changed.Coronella: Smooth snakes: weak oral secretion, generally described as non-venomous. Left as non-venomous
